newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - EMU hopeful Portugal good outside bet.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - EMU hopeful Portugal good outside bet.

text.p: Investors hunting down convergence trades should look at Portugal, the wallflower of so-called Club Med economies and one which a growing band of economists say will meet the criteria for monetary union.

Portugal's euro aspirations are often overlooked by markets which tend to focus on neighbouring Spain. Scepticism about its chances of joining a single European currency without Spain mean spread narrowing will be bumpy, they said.
"There does look to be good value in Portugal where it is now," said Yamaichi market economist Juli Collins-Thompson.

"Spreads could narrow significantly over the next few months as it becomes appparent to international markets that fundamentals are improving...and it will be able to meet the Maastricht criteria," added Collins-Thompson.

By 1200 GMT, the 10-year Portuguese/German spread was at 118 basis points. Just six weeks ago, it was at 88 basis points. It has widened on the latest bout of fears of a delay to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Collins-Thompson expected the spread to move below 100 basis points in the next few months and below 50 basis points in the next year or so.
Analysts said Portugal was well on course to meet the Maastricht criteria.

The Portuguese government expects a public sector deficit of 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997, the year in which aspiring member nations will be judged for EMU. Under new Eurostat rules it forecast the country's debt to GDP (Gross Domestic Product) ratio at 64.3 percent this year.

Under Maastricht rules, candidate countries need a debt to GDP ratio of just 60 percent, but almost equal importance is given to the fact that a ratio is falling. The deficit must be 3.0 percent of GDP.
The EU's 15 member states will decide in spring 1998 which countries have qualified for the first round of EMU.
Attention turned to Portugal's debt markets on Thursday after the European Investment Bank issued an escudo bond which may be redenominated in euros.

Analysts said while strictly speaking there was nothing to stop Portugal from joining EMU in the first round without Spain, provided it met the criteria, market cynicism of the reality means spread narrowing will be an erratic process.

"It's going to be difficult for the market to distinguish between Portugal, Spain and Italy," said Ian Gunner, senior economist at Chase in London. "There is the belief that if Spain is not allowed in, Portugal won't want to."
With a large proportion of Portugal's trade tied to Spain, there is the fear it may suffer competitively if its Iberian neighbour devalues the peseta outside EMU.
"But I suspect Spain will pursue reasonable policies with a view to going into EMU in a few years' time," added Gunner.

Southern European economist at Salomon Brothers, Jose Luis Alzola, agreed that while it was likely Portugal would meet the Maastricht criteria, political manoevering meant that would not necessarily guarantee entry in the first wave.
"I think Portugal will probably meet the numerical criteria for EMU at the beginning. But the problem will be how politicians interpret the sustainability aspect," he said.
Alzola said Portugal had a 50/50 chance of being in the first wave of EMU, and if it didn't make that, it had a good chance of entering within one or two years.
He saw the spread narrowing to around 75 basis points by year end, but said the move would be far from smooth.
Gunner was more wary. "I expect spreads to range trade around here and may even widen further in the next few weeks," he said, citing further EMU delay talk as the sticking point.
